title: Zoo Animals
strapline: Feeding time at the zoo — mind the lions.
intent: Animals are one of the first great loves of early childhood, and a zoo world gives that fascination somewhere rich to grow.
Sorting, feeding and housing the animals is natural mathematics — grouping, counting, comparing big and small.
Caring for the animals — feeding, cleaning, keeping them safe — stretches empathy and responsibility.
Animal names, sounds, homes and diets pour in as vocabulary and early knowledge of the living world.
The zoo becomes a stage for stories: escaped animals, new babies, a vet's visit, a busy feeding round.
implementation: Offer a good range of animals plus open-ended materials — blocks, fences, containers, natural bits — so children build the enclosures themselves.
Sit alongside and wonder: 'I wonder which animals should live together, and which need to be kept apart.'
Model the keeper's care talk: 'The lion looks hungry — what does he need? Let's check he has clean water.'
Feed in real knowledge lightly — what each animal eats, where it comes from, the sounds it makes.
Bring in maths without a worksheet: how many penguins, which enclosure has more, sort the big cats from the small.
Add signs, tickets and a map so there is a reason to make marks and read them.
Follow a child's animal passion — dinosaurs, big cats, minibeasts — and let the zoo become about that.
key_questions: Which animals should live together, and which need their own space?
What does this animal need to be happy and healthy?
How many animals are in this enclosure — which one has more?
What sound does it make, and where in the world does it come from?
What job does the zookeeper need to do next?

impact.text: Children sort and group the animals — by size, by home, by kind — and explain their groupings.
Children count the animals and compare enclosures, using 'more', 'fewer' and 'the same'.
Children act as keepers and vets, caring for the animals and playing out feeding, cleaning and rescue stories.
Children name animals and talk about what they eat, the sounds they make and where they live.
Children build and adapt enclosures with fences and blocks, solving how to keep each animal safely in.
Children show gentle care for the animals and cooperate with others sharing the zoo.

enhancements: Blocks, fences, tubes and natural materials for building enclosures and dens.
Small containers for food and water, and 'food' (seeds, shredded paper, pom-poms).
A vet's kit for a poorly-animal day.
Zoo tickets, a map, signs and a mark-making station for keepers' notes.
Non-fiction animal books and pictures to fuel real knowledge.
A sorting challenge: hoops or trays labelled by size, habitat or diet.

playing_exploring: Children follow a deep, genuine interest in animals and play it out in their own way.
They test and arrange the world — grouping, housing and feeding their creatures.
active_learning: Children take on the keeper's responsibilities and see the feeding round or rescue through.
creating_thinking: Children decide which animals belong together and why, and invent stories about their zoo.
